While I'm still in favor of merging this as it's very useful from the command line (`gh help reference`) it unfortunately does not survive the translation to markdown well for use on the manual site; it ends up being very garbled with all formatting and indentation lost.

I see three options:

- porting this to generate markdown (instead of directly using `ColorScheme` functions) and then running it through glamour
- porting it to generate markdown and printing the raw markdown on the CLI
- tweaking the formatting so it looks at least intelligible when it becomes markdown

I'm leaning towards the first option; in general the help topic system is meant to do double duty of CLI and HTML help and we're only going to want _more_ markdown formatting in help topics, not less.

I'm happy to augment this to output markdown.

I've gotten this generating markdown in my local environment, but some shortcomings of glamour are making the output less than ideal; the primary issue is the inability to manually linebreak which I'd like for the flag usage lists. I'll explore using tables or blockquotes for that.

Either way I have to focus on other things today but I'll circle back to this.

I've pushed commits for having this output markdown. I had to make some trade-offs but I think it looks acceptable; most importantly, it should look ok on the manual website.

issue_context.title: "reference" help topic to list all commands and subcommands
issue_context.body:
### Searching for a particular gh CLI command can be cumbersome 

There must be a separate command such as 'gh manual' which lists all the GitHub CLI commands and its usage.

### Proposed solution: New command 'gh manual'

It will benefit all the users to quickly skim through and find the needful command in few seconds.
comments:
Thanks for raising this!

All of the top level commands are listed in `gh help`; are you talking about listing all of the subcommands, too?

> Thanks for raising this!
> 
> All of the top level commands are listed in `gh help`; are you talking about listing all of the subcommands, too?

Yes all of the commands and their relevant syntax

I think what you are looking for is 
```bash
man gh
```
which appears to be incomplete currently.

> I think what you are looking for is
> 
> ```shell
> man gh
> ```
> 
> which appears to be incomplete currently.

Yes! 

`man gh` command will do the needful.

> which appears to be incomplete currently.

What is missing? I just took a cursory glance and see all of the stuff that shipped with 1.0.

> > which appears to be incomplete currently.
> 
> What is missing? I just took a cursory glance and see all of the stuff that shipped with 1.0.

A help command should list all possible sub commands with their possible uses and syntax

I think it's important to keep the current help pages succinct; but I'd potentially be open to a `gh help reference` help topic that enumerates every command and subcommand so folks can grep it and then look up specific help docs once they know what subcommands are there. I'm curious what @ampinsk thinks.

> A help command should list all possible sub commands with their possible uses and syntax

I don't necessarily agree that the main help command should list all possible sub-command and their syntax. If we look at `man git` or `git --help`, which I think has well-designed documentation system, all possible `git *` sub-commands are not explicitly listed. Instead, individual help sub-pages are referenced, like we do in `man gh`, and the user is guided to dive into the help for specific sub-commands, such as `man gh-pr`, to discover the full extent of GitHub CLI functionality.

If this wasn't clear already, then I'm up for reshaping our documentation to make it clearer.
Agree that our help pages should probably relatively stay structured as they are now, but definitely open to a command that lists them in full: `gh help reference` makes sense to me!
I can jump on this one!

@mislav I wanted to take some time to address my original comment as it indirectly resulted in your comment.

Here is the version of the entire gh man page I have locally. This is newer than my original comment, but probably not current. 

```
gh(1)Oct(2020)                                                                                                  gh(1)Oct(2020)



Auto generated by spf13/cobra


NAME
       gh - GitHub CLI



SYNOPSIS
       gh   [flags]



DESCRIPTION
       Work seamlessly with GitHub from the command line.



OPTIONS
       --help[=false]      Show help for command


       --version[=false]      Show gh version



EXAMPLE
              $ gh issue create
              $ gh repo clone cli/cli
              $ gh pr checkout 321





SEE ALSO
       gh-alias(1),  gh-api(1),  gh-auth(1), gh-completion(1), gh-config(1), gh-gist(1), gh-issue(1), gh-pr(1), gh-release(1),
       gh-repo(1)



HISTORY
       6-Oct-2020 Auto generated by spf13/cobra
```

While other pages are referenced, they have no descriptions. By contrast, let's look at a small piece of git's man page where it goes through their commands:

```GIT COMMANDS
       We divide Git into high level ("porcelain") commands and low level ("plumbing") commands.

HIGH-LEVEL COMMANDS (PORCELAIN)
       We separate the porcelain commands into the main commands and some ancillary user utilities.

   Main porcelain commands
       git-add(1)
           Add file contents to the index.

       git-am(1)
           Apply a series of patches from a mailbox.

       git-archive(1)
           Create an archive of files from a named tree.

       git-bisect(1)
           Use binary search to find the commit that introduced a bug.

       git-branch(1)
           List, create, or delete branches.

       git-bundle(1)
           Move objects and refs by archive.

       git-checkout(1)
           Switch branches or restore working tree files.

       git-cherry-pick(1)
           Apply the changes introduced by some existing commits.
```

This is the level of detail I usually expect from manual pages. This expectation is what led to my original comment, "which appears to be incomplete currently." Manuals are generally supposed to contain highly detailed and unambiguous information about a given program/tool/api. They are not high level overviews, but literal instruction manuals for users.

@mayt-moonboy Thanks for taking the time to illustrate your point. I fully agree, and I will try to incrementally make steps to bring our man pages closer to the quality level of git man pages. 👍 

Right now, they seem rudimentary because they are. We're only taking what our CLI framework generates and not improving that in any way. Over time, we saw that we need to take documentation matters into our own hands, because what was provided for us is sub-par.
